utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, appearing for Mr. Naser Oric together with Mr. John Jones. Joining us today are our legal assistant, Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. So before we admit in the witness, there are a couple of matters I would like to raise. You will recall that some time back, some time back, we granted -- we admitted in evidence two Rule 92 bis (C) statements; one was a written decision and the other one was an oral ruling. You will recall the two persons involved. Now, the motion, when filed, and that is on the 27th of September, was filed confidentially, with the consequence that the statements that the Prosecution was seeking to have admitted under Rule 92(C) were not public and were not treated as such by the Trial Chamber. With hindsight, we really don't see why the two statements ought to remain confidential, and why they shouldn't, in other words, become public domain. I am raising this issue formally so that I have a feedback. Of course, Mr. Wubben or Ms. Richardson, if you still have good reason to show why these two documents, two statements, should remain confidential, the Trial Chamber would entertain your views, hear the Defence, and then obviously take a stand. But if you don't, then we can cut the discussion short and we can issue an order making these two statements public, in spite of the confidentiality that was given to them when they were first filed as part of the confidential motion of the 27th of September, 2004. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, will you please give me the time until the after -- until after the first or second break to make an oral submission in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You will have the first break. The second relates to a most recent filing in our case, and that's a confidential Prosecution request for the issuances of a subpoena ad testificandum with an ex parte annex. I suppose you have received it already. Is there any objection on your part for the issuance of the subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, none. We agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the motion is being granted. There will not be a written decision. It's been granted already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've been informed that the formality required for the issuance of a subpoena usually requires a written decision, so there will be, for all intents and purposes, a written decision along the lines of the oral decision that we have just given, all right? Yes, any further preliminaries before we admit the witness? Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I will raise two issues briefly, the first concerning tomorrow's testimony of Witness Miladinovic. There has been no reference to any protective measures; therefore, I am mentioning his name in public. Yesterday, we received proofing notes from the OTP that are entirely illegible, and we asked for a new copy. At 20 past 9.00 today we received a new set of proofing notes stating that the witness is, illegible [as interpreted], can't read or write, stating further that he is short-sighted 11 degrees. I wish to say that again we have yet another witness appearing who suddenly becomes illegible as soon as he is here in The Hague to testify. The fact is this witness has been interviewed twice by the OTP; the first time in March 2000 and the second time in 2003. In neither of these statements is there any reference at all to the fact that the witness is illiterate. The witness signed both statements as well as the dates of the statements. He recognised the numbers on the photographs and described exactly the content of the plaque that was smashed in Kravica, the memorial plaque. I must express my concern yet again at the way the OTP is conducting their case. If the witness really is illiterate, as has been suggested, then there must have been something in his prior statements to confirm that. The question of literacy is a routine issue that is always raised in all legal proceedings anywhere in the world. The fact is that the OTP has yet again succeeded in making us waste our time by putting us in a position to cross-examine this witness in a way that is not adequate. Your Honours, rest assured that I would have prepared my cross-examination in a totally different way had I known at the outset that the witness was illiterate. Be that as it may, I will present all the necessary documents for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. However, I must yet again plead with the Trial Chamber to put a stop to these unacceptable practices on the part of the OTP. At the very least, we must be told ahead of time that a witness is short-sighted or illiterate, the first reason being to be given a chance to properly prepare my cross-examination, and the second reason being that I have a chance to look into whether the witness really is illiterate or short-sighted or not. Therefore, we would like the OTP to check the literacy of all future witnesses, and to please forward this information by the Christmas break, or as soon as otherwise possible. Believe me, Your Honours, I will look into these facts carefully and carry out my own investigations into these issues. Therefore, if this initial may please be discussed briefly, and then I would like to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who is going to respond, Mr. Wubben or Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour. I object to the qualification of wasting of time regarding this witness. Counsel had -- counsel of the Defence has already dealt with it in a previous time on cross, and cross-examination is the appropriate situation in which counsel can check out whether or not someone is illiterate. Let me put forward that there is no legal basis to request or demand from the Prosecution to check out every witness, whether or not he or she is illiterate. It is of importance whether or not this witness can tell or confirm or clarify details, facts, for you as a -- you as Judges. That's the nucleus, and I see no -- also not from the case law, any demand towards the Prosecution to provide this information in advance in such a way when it is not available. As it was for me available, I confirmed Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that towards Defence counsel through the proofing notes. Let me also underline that when a witness cannot read or write, it's here about oral evidence, and they know it's also beneficial to confront a witness with a -- with some written notes or whatever, document. But the same when it comes to equality of arms is addressing the Prosecution side, when we are also having this disadvantage. And again, in addition, then a witness is still able to recognise pictures, photographs, and so on. I see no prejudice, with a view to equality of arms. I see no legal basis for putting such a condition on the Prosecution side. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Second point, Ms. Vidovic, unless you want to reply to Mr. Wubben's remarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honours. The legal basis is provided by Rule 54, envisaging that the accused has the right to a fair trial, and the right for every witness, therefore, that implies that we have the right to cross-examine a witness on all relevant circumstances, including the presentation of documents. It surely must be a waste of our time if we're expected to prepare this witness by going through 10 or 15 documents and through a great number of other documents in the archive in order to prepare our cross-examination. As for the fact that they are not duty-bound by the Rules to submit this sort of information to us, I leave that to the Trial Chamber to decide for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Second point?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second point is of a more serious nature, yet more serious nature, I should say, Your Honours, the first one being quite serious as well. It goes to the testimony of Mr. Ratko Nikolic, and today's witness, Nikola Popovic. I need not remind the Trial Chamber that Naser Oric has been accused of the most serious crimes, including murder. For our information in relation to on-site investigations, post-mortems that were conducted and exhumations is of great relevance. Your Honours, I would like you to refer to the case law of your respective countries, or any court of law throughout the world. I am entirely certain that none of these courts could make rulings if they were in no position to look into the post-mortems or exhumation reports, as well as any other details in relation to these and referenced in witness testimonies. In the case of Mr. Kostadin Popovic's testimony, this is of the utmost relevance. We know, based on the testimonies of at least two or three different witnesses, that an exhumation was carried out of a body purported to be that of Kostadin Popovic. In my letter of the 17th of November, 2004, I addressed the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska and the first instance court in Zvornik seeking to obtain all the relevant documents in relation to the exhumation of Mr. Popovic's body. The file number with that court is 345/95. The reply was that the case was forwarded to the district prosecutor's office of Zvornik, or rather, Bijeljina, which then took over the case. On the 4th of December, 2004, I submitted a letter to the district public prosecutor's office, office of Bijeljina, in which I asked for the following: "In order to submit relevant evidence, in my capacity as defence counsel for Mr. Naser Oric, and pursuant to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina I envisage the cooperation of all courts, and pursuant to the law on freedom of information and access to information, I request that I be forwarded a photograph, A2, which is part of the accompanying evidence in relation to the exhumation of Mr. Kostadin Popovic conducted by Mr. Zoran Popovic. The text below the photograph number 2 is a paper containing the personal data of the victim after the blanket was opened." I went through all the details of this entire file, after which the public district prosecutor from Bijeljina kindly informed me as follows: "Further to your request for submitting documents, I hereby inform you that as for the documents at the disposal of this prosecutor's office in relation to the case of Naser Oric, we do not have any data in relation to this. The documents relating to that person have been forwarded in part to the International Criminal Tribunal for war crimes in The Hague, and these documents have never been returned." My office talked directly to the prosecutor, asking for further clarifications, and he replied that he only had a copy which have been submitted to us. Therefore, Your Honours, the way it looks to us now, we have a perfectly clear indication that the OTP, at some point, obtained these documents and that these were never disclosed to us. They failed to disclose to us a fundamental piece of evidence in relation to Kostadin Popovic's testimony. Likewise, it seems that we have been prevented in obtaining these documents from the original source. The Bijeljina prosecutor requested that I come in person to go through whatever files they had, claiming that he would make them all available to me for inspection, but saying also that he could not give me something that they simply didn't have. Your Honours, I wish to draw your attention today to something that is within my rights as Defence counsel in this case. It seems to me that from the very outset, I have been defending my client with my hands tied at my back, and therefore I only have one free hand to use to further pursue the matter for. We believe that the OTP should submit to us all these documents and similar documents so that we could have proper cross-examination, or else there will be such errors of fact in this trial that justice will simply not be done. As for myself, in my capacity as Defence counsel, I definitely wish to take no further part in anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben or Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can respond in part to Defence counsel. Your Honour, with respect to the testimony of the witness today who will be continuing, Nikola Popovic, who is the son of Kostadin Popovic, the victim or the person -- the deceased person to whom Defence counsel is referring, I don't want to make any assumptions, but it appears to me as though the Defence will be seeking to cross-examine this particular witness about his father's autopsy. And if I'm wrong, the Defence can correct me. It's my understanding that we have disclosed information to the Defence, and I would ask for the Court's indulgence, at least until the break, so we can determine exactly which documents were disclosed to them, what part of the autopsy or medical records were in fact disclosed or which ones were not, so we can provide an accurate record to the Court of what was provided. And in addition, the doctor himself who performed the autopsy will be testifying after the Christmas break, so the Defence will have adequate opportunity, though I am not in any way instructing the Defence not to attempt to cross-examine this present witness with respect to the autopsy of his father. I'm just saying that the person who conducted the autopsy will be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about the report itself, the official records of the autopsy which the office in Bijeljina maintains has forwarded to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And which the Defence claims to have never received?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I honestly do not have a response to that concern at this time. I do know that the Office of the Prosecutor did disclose information about certain victims, and I couldn't tell you offhand now at this moment whether or not we received documents from Bijeljina and whether or not those were the documents that we disclosed or failed to disclose to the Defence. Again, Your Honour, I ask the Court's indulgence. I don't know off the top of my head whether or not this was done. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to be as brief as possible. We did receive certain information, and we pursued this information, totally heterogenous information as far as two different witness statements are concerned, we carried out our investigation. We are looking for an entire file, which means the record of an on-site investigation, the report by an investigating judge, and what exactly was found. We are talking about a specific exhibit here. We have information, on the one hand, and, on the other, evidence that we are entitled to inspect, including a post-mortem report that was handed over to the court, including everything that was given over to the court in Zvornik. You do agree that we have the right to inspect all of these. And we know exactly what the information is that we have been given, and we know what our rights are and what we are entitled to in order to properly defend our client. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I'm not contesting the fact that the Defence is entitled to certain information. It's not that at all. It's just at this time I don't have a list of the documents that were disclosed with respect to the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will suspend the sitting for a few minutes so that we have consultations outside the courtroom. We'll be back in a matter of minutes, so please stay here. --- Break taken at 2.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have deliberated and we come to the following conclusions unanimously. I'll start with the first issue raised by Madam Vidovic. We do not believe that we can impose an obligation on the Defence along the lines suggested by -- on the Prosecution along the lines suggested by the Defence, namely, to verify between now and the recess which of the remaining witnesses are illiterate and which are not, and to hand down a proper list. We don't believe that the Prosecution is under a legal obligation to do so. However, we do believe that this is a matter of courtesy. We do believe that the complaint raised by Madam Vidovic, namely, that not knowing that this person allegedly was illiterate, she prepared her defence questions on the assumption that she could show him documents which he could read and answer about promptly, only to find out that this is not possible because you maintain that he is illiterate, we don't believe that this is fair. So it's a question of making the best use of the limited resources that each one of you have, and as you know, the Defence, when compared to the Prosecution, has less resources than you have. You are always in a better position to know whether a witness is literate or not. I would take it that your investigators questioning the witnesses should enter into the record whether -- if the person is illiterate, I think that some way you should have it. And I would advise you - I would advise you, although we cannot bind you - I would advise you to do the exercise that has been suggested - not necessarily up to Christmas but do it at your earliest - and if you have the information, then pass it on to the Defence. We say it's a matter of courtesy, first and foremost, and of course it is a matter of courtesy, first and foremost. However, it's also a matter of being pragmatic and practical, because there is nothing to stop Mr. Jones or Ms. Vidovic, or whoever, on a particular day when they hear, or they come to know that the witness that they are supposed to start cross-examining today or tomorrow is illiterate saying, We were not prepared for this, we need to reprogramme the whole defence approach and strategy, questions, et cetera, and we may find ourselves coming here only to go back home after five minutes because of this unfortunate problem. So I think I have been more than clear. I think I have been more than clear. We don't see any question of equality, fairness, or legal obligation here. We just see it's a matter of being courteous and being practical. Otherwise, there will be consequences. Otherwise, there will be consequences. Not consequences from the Trial Chamber vis-a-vis imposing you, consequences having one day sitting maybe more simply, simply, simply blown up; you know, ruined. That disposes of the first matter. The second matter, we agree, the three of us, with Ms. Vidovic that this is a serious matter, and we appreciate the fact that she has raised this matter, because indeed we agree that the accused should have at his disposal all the information, all the data, that are provided for under the Rules in order to be able to provide for his own adequate defence. Now, we have taken note of the fact that you seem to not be in a position to state here and now whether the document -- am I wrong, Ms. Richardson? Have you got the information now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you. I was able to ascertain within the last few minutes that what we have disclosed, and we will look into that document that Ms. Vidovic has been referring to -- that, we don't know. But I do know that the forensic report was -- on Mr. Kostadin Popovic was disclosed on the 25th of June, 2003. Then there was an autopsy protocol that was also provided on the 22nd of April, 2003. We're looking into that specific report that the Defence has just raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree, Madam Vidovic, that these two documents have been disclosed when stated?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot confirm this until I have checked it, because I have heard things like this many times. However, my point is something else. They have disclosed information about the autopsy conducted by Dr. Stankovic. What I'm referring to is the entire court file which should contain a record of the on-site investigation, a record of the autopsy, a record of the objects found. And this is something I have certainly never received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the question is this: You need time, obviously, Ms. Richardson, to verify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have got two options. One option is to go back to our chambers and give you all the time you require, and then come back, and we take it up from there; in the meantime, we will not be starting or continuing with the testimony of Mr. Popovic. The consequence would be that we would certainly not finish with Mr. Popovic today, and we certainly will not even start with the next witness tomorrow. So we have discussed this in the light that certain documents are available, and hoping that the other main document that Madam Vidovic is referring to may be located and disclosed. Can we proceed with the testimony of Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will put questions to Mr. Popovic in a certain way, but to say the least, if they have these documents in their possession, as transpires from the letter from the public prosecutor, I would like them to disclose this to us so that we can use it in our cross-examination of the next witness, that is, Dr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, we will disclose this information. As soon as we determine whether we do have it and it is in our possession, we will have it to the Defence immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with the other caveat - I'm making it very clear on behalf of the Trial Chamber - that if this document indeed exists. And if, once disclosed, it transpires that Madam Vidovic and Mr. Jones require the return of Mr. Popovic here to be confronted with any new matter/issue that results from this document, then he will have to come back. Am I Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond making myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're making yourself perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just say I think Your Honours have been very clear about this being a physical file, an autopsy report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Indeed, Your Honours. But that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you what it is like in my country, but I can't tell you what it is -- I have seen like it. Actually, I have seen like it in other cases, yes. I can tell you what it is like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I simply emphasise that, because my learned friend keeps referring to information. It's not information we want, it's not summaries, it's not the witness statements referring to the point. It's the physical court report with photographs, autopsy notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's what we call an inquest in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Clearly, it's whatever the Defence has referred to it as the file. I may have misused the word and used "information," but it's clearly the documents that they were seeking. I was just given a note with respect to the Zvornik report that I believe is what Defence is seeking. It's my understanding that it was requested by us but never received, and we are looking for verification of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we'll continue, and we'll take this matter up -- the matter is not closed, in other words. We'll take the matter up once we have more information from you, and once we are in a better position to make a proper assessment. Any further matters? I see none -- yes, Madam Vidovic, none? Madam Usher, could you please admit the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please stand up. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. I hope you have had some time to relax after the beginning of the testimony that you gave last Monday. I want to make sure, first and foremost, that you have not maintained any contact with anyone on the matters related to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that no one has approached you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to make you aware that you are still testifying under oath; in other words, in terms of the solemn declaration that you made last Monday that you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will now continue with the examination-in-chief, and then you are going to be - hopefully we'll start today - cross-examined by the Defence. Madam Richardson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Richardson: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to conclude with your testimony that you began on Monday as indicated by Judge Agius. When we concluded on Monday, you were describing the -- you were testifying about the defence line, and you also stated that there were two villages that had been attacked, and that your mother-in-law and sister-in-law were killed. And I believe these villages were Magasici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation? I think I would still suggest that you repeat your question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I am, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I kindly ask you to repeat your question, or if you want I can read it out for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you reading it out is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Popovic, when we left off on Monday, you were testifying about the defence lines; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you also stated that there were two villages that had been attacked; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that during these attacks, your mother-in-law and sister-in-law were killed; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you tell us again the names of these two villages? Was one Magasici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Magasici, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what was the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now I hand him back to you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask for the usher's assistance. If you could please show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 455, which is a map that we had been using.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, if you would like a look at the map, I believe you already circled Jezestica on the map. Is Magasici, the other village that you just mentioned that was attacked, also visible on this map?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could just point to both villages.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jezestica. Magasici. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was it after the attack on these villages that the defence line, the Kravica defence line, was established?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it appears as though Jezestica is also part of the defence line. Could you explain why -- what were the circumstances of Jezestica? In other words, were there people still living in this village, and you found -- and that it was found necessary to establish the defence line along the borders of Jezestica as well?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were still living in Jezestica and the surrounding hamlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions with respect to this map at the moment. Now, I would ask, with respect to the facilities located in Kravica, I believe you may have testified previously on Monday that there was a kitchen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what this kitchen was used for, and where was this kitchen located?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kitchen was in the school. It was used to feed the village. The village, the soldiers, the civilians, whoever wanted to, came and had lunch here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when this kitchen in the school was set up?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where the food that was kept in this kitchen and distributed to the villagers and the soldiers of Kravica, where this food supply came from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the food came from; I'm not aware of that. There were people who toured the villages, and there were people who had Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond large quantities of potatoes or beans, and this was brought to the kitchen so that the population could be fed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, if you know, was there any person in charge of this kitchen, or more than one, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cooks working in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if weapons or any type of military equipment was kept in this kitchen or in the school?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there was nothing like that in the kitchen where the food was; however, I didn't go into the other rooms, and I don't know what was in the other rooms in these premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there did come a time that another -- an attack on a village by the name of Glogova took place.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in December; I don't know the exact date, but it was somewhere between the 20th and the 23rd, around then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the result of this attack? And who attacked Glogova, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac-Kravica road was cut off as a result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who was responsible for this attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the Muslims from Srebrenica, led by Naser Oric at their head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did this attack affect the villages in the immediate vicinity of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did have an effect because they cut off the Kravica-Bratunac road. And they surrounded us. They surrounded Glogova, Konjevic Polje, Magasici, Jezestica, Srebrenica, so we were totally surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this affect the utility, such as electricity, in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as Glogova was cut off, we no longer had electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher's assistance, with the same map to be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, if you can, when the map is placed on the ELMO, please indicate where Glogova is located on this map.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find it? Could you circle -- and I should ask, what was the ethnic makeup of this village back in 1992, when it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I might as well say it. That village was attacked twice in 1992, at least, so I suppose that you better distinguish between one and the other, or at least be more specific, because the ethnic composition certainly changed after the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will inquire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, how many times, to your knowledge, was Glogova attacked?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but I know about the attack in December, when the Bratunac-Kravica road was cut off. I can't tell you about other attacks. There were attacks, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- when was this? Did you just say -- what time of year was this? What month?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, in December, between the 20th and the 24th of December, for three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time of that attack in December of 1992, were there Serbs living in that village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were controlling the road above the village. There were no Serbs in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the village itself, was there anyone killed as a result of this attack, in Glogova itself?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you show us on the map where the road was cut off leading to Bratunac. And if you could, with a red pen, just - thank you - indicate.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't follow on the monitor. All right. Leave it there. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, I'm just trying to follow this witness' evidence, which seems to be that Muslims are attacking Muslims in Glogova. I must admit, I find it thoroughly confusing, if that could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Richardson still has to pursue that matter. I wouldn't comment more on it. I think she's still got to pursue it, and if she doesn't, I will. Yes. Again, I could not follow on the monitor from the beginning when he started charting. The question was where the road was cut off leading to Bratunac. Is it where you put the circle around the name Gradac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from Hranca to Avdagina Njive. But I can't find the names of these places here. This used to be called Gradac before, Tresnija [phoen], Gradac, Njive. That's what it was called before. But the only name I can find now is Gradac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the witness put a circle around the name Gradac which is shown on the map between Agici and Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Nothing further on this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you indicated, when you testified earlier that Glogova -- there were no Serbs living in Glogova but it had been attacked, could you explain for the Trial Chamber what you mean by -- exactly what happened, and the significance of Glogova being attacked, if you know.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know how it was. Glogova belonged to Bratunac. I don't know much about Glogova. I know that before it used to be Muslim, and that it was cleansed at the beginning of the war. And after that, there was a line above Glogova that was held by Serb soldiers. Above Glogova, up there, there were places where our soldiers were, and in December the Muslims attacked there and cut off the road from Hranca to Avdagina Njive and Graca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say where there were Serb soldiers, these Serb soldiers that you were just referring to, were they part of the defence line, or were they Serb soldiers from another area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That was not the Kravica area. This belonged to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did Kravica do following the Glogova attack, and specifically with respect to the defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kravica set up a line as far as Avdagina Njive, Avdagina Njive and then across to Mandici, Magasici, Jezestica, Siljkovici, and all the way around. Siljkovici, Marici, Jezero, the Bacici dam, Munecici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would just like to bring you to the attack on Kravica itself. What do you recall -- do you recall what day that occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that day significant?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the Serb Orthodox Christmas; it's an important feast day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, is there any special festivities or things that someone of Serb ethnicity would be doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the eve of Christmas, we slaughter pigs, and then you usually wake up early on the 7th of January, and you have breakfast and you celebrate throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that day, do you recall what you were doing when the attack took place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, or rather, that night and day, I worked in the bakery. I roasted pigs for the soldiers who were on the front line and for the rest of the village. Whoever wanted some, we roasted pigs for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you become aware that the village was being attacked? What time was this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was early in the morning, between 6.00 and 6.30, when the first sounds of shooting were heard. In the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the direction -- where the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first shots that were heard early - I was in the bakery - it came from Marici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you with anyone?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were four of us in the bakery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these four individuals?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four of my colleagues. We worked together in the bakery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything else with respect to the attack that led you to believe that the village was under attack? And specifically, if I have the Court's permission to lead the witness a bit, was there an alarm that was given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Marici was attacked, when the attack began to spread to Siljkovici and the rest of the defence line, then a siren went off and an alarm was sounded to warn people that the village was under attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was -- and what did most of the villagers do at the time of this alarm?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of this alarm, when it started, people assembled outside the school building in Kravica. All those who were able went to the defence line to help, because the conflict had already spread to all the villages around Kravica. When Marici fell, in Kravica, around the school building and the bakery, you could no longer walk around freely, because the shooting began and three or four people were killed in Kravica itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were your family members, such as your father, your mother, and your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all inside the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they do once the village was under attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came in front of the school building. My father went straight to the defence line; my mother was still near the house, until the time came to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My grandfather was with us in the bakery throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time that you left the bakery?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until we started to flee. I stayed in the bakery, and then the time came to go and then we were all off to the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the bakery, prior to your leaving, were you able to see what the other villagers were doing, or if there were any wounded persons in the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning, around 8.00 or half past 8.00, the first victim fell, Milovan Nikolic from Omici. The alarm was sounded and he headed for the defence line at Jezero. When the four or five of them left, I was still outside the bakery. The men had gone, but before an hour elapsed, they brought him back. And by the time they brought his body into the school building, he had already died. The Muslims had got behind the line at Jezero and they ambushed the help that was on its way to Jezero. And that's where they killed him. This is midway between Kravica and Jezero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that Marici was the first, I believe, village that you said was under attack. Could you see this village from where you were?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the bakery you could see the first house, you could see it from the bakery where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that it began to burn. And when they started firing on Kravica, you couldn't walk about safely. And I know that several people were wounded in the school courtyard, outside the school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that there came a time that you left the bakery, and this was when you fled Kravica, the town itself. Who left the bakery with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My friends, Krsto Timic, Vaso Gavric, Zoran Eric, and myself left. And once we had set out, some civilians joined us on the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your grandfather also accompany you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I left the bakery, I said, Grandpa, come on, let's go, it's time to run. And he said, Where am I supposed to run to? And I said, Let's run to the Drina River. And he said, Listen, grandson, there's no way I can reach the river, I don't stand a chance, I can't get there. If there was a car we could use, perhaps. But the snow was deep and it was impossible to reach the Drina by car. He started crying, and he said, I'm not leaving this place. I'm 82 years old. I never harmed anyone. I pleaded with him, Come on, we'll carry you, we'll get you out of here. And he said, Come on, it would be pointless for me to leave. And then I tried to convince him but he just wouldn't agree, and I had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What direction did you flee?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fled towards Opravdici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you meet anyone else as you were fleeing towards Opravdici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean civilians?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By the time we reached Opravdici - this is a hill from which you could see the surrounding villages - Jezestica, Kajici, Siljkovici, Marici; you could see all those villages from there - there were already people there that had assembled in Opravdici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any family members with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I left Opravdici and headed for Macinovici, I found my mother who had left before me with their lady friends. They had left as early as 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when you encountered your mother?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Midway between Opravdici and Colakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you remained or you passed through the village of Colakovici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anybody --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed in Colakovici. When we reached the hill of Colakovici, there were quite a number of civilians there, and we waited until the army started to withdraw and then we all headed for the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Opravdici, which is further down from Colakovici, you could see that Jezestica was burning, and Kajici, the asphalt road there, the houses next to the asphalt road in Kravica, Siljkovici, you could see it all quite clearly from Opravdici. The whole thing was burning. Brezak and Mandici. Mandici was beginning to burn too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance with the same map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could point on that map, Mr. Popovic, to Opravdici, and tell us if that's the village that you were able to observe the burning that was taking place in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I saw Jezestica, Kajici, Siljkovici, Marici, Brezak, I saw these villages burning from Opravdici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also testified that the attack came from the village of Marici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marici, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know which other villages after Marici was under attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marici was the first village to be attacked, near Kravica. The first attack that I heard was in Marici, and from there it spread to Siljkovici, and from Siljkovici to Jezestica, Jezero, the Bacici dam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you, but why don't you use the pointer and just point to the villages that were under attack after Marici.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marici and then Siljkovici. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which village followed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jezestica. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then which other village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Magasici. [Indicates]. Magasici, Avdagina Njive, Mandici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the pattern of attack was Marici, then Jezestica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marici, Siljkovici, Jezestica, Magasici, Avdagina Njive, Mandici, and then it spread to Sandici, Jezero, the Bacici dam, the lower dam and the upper dam, Banjevici, Bacici. So the whole area was under attack, all these villages that I've pointed out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all with respect to -- Madam Usher, with respect to this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people died in the village of Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Siljkovici, 13 to 15 people were killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there anything significant that you recall about this village during the attack, anything particular that took place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That attack on that day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. These 15 people, were they all related?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a big family, the Radovic family, that was their last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they do anything in particular with respect to holding off the attack on the other villages, or allowing the villagers --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm just leading a bit to get some additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think so on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, but I think it's not clear-cut so I wanted your input. Go ahead and lead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the 13 to 15 people that you just testified about who were related, did they do anything significant during the attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They held off the line. They stayed there until the time came to -- well, they helped Kravica, because Siljkovici is the biggest hill and the nearest one to Kravica. The distance is not even 100 metres, as the crow flies, between Siljkovici and the center of Kravica. That was the fiercest attack, the one up there. And the entire Radovic family were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have one last question with respect to what you were able to observe when you were in Opravdici. Is Opravdici located on the hill, which is why you were able to see the other villages, including Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to getting or arriving at the Drina River while you were fleeing, did you encounter Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we came across Serb soldiers who were on their way to help Kravica. That was on the way down to Drina, between Colakovici and Sopotnik, midway between the forest called Strugovi. There's a village there, and we met about 50 soldiers who were on their way to help Kravica, but it was too late by then. And we told them that it all was in vain because Kravica was ablaze. But they pressed on and came back together with our army when it left Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "army," do you mean the men that were on the defence line?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a very leading question. If he could just be asked what he means by "army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase your question, please, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "army," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the people on the defence line, the people from the village of Kravica, the army that was on its way to help Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you saw your father again?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw my father again. After he had left to go to the front line, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you told, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I came down to the road, the soldiers had already reached Sopotnik. I asked if anyone had seen my father because I realised that he wasn't there, and they all said, We really can't say. We were all shattered. It was dark by then. It was 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening. A bus came, and we got onto the bus and drove off to Bratunac. The next day when we all came together in Bratunac, a neighbour of mine from Kravica, Mijo Gavric, who was the last person to see my father on the line, came up to me and said that my father had been captured alive. At first I couldn't believe, but he said, Yes, he was, I was with him, he was captured alive, and I managed to escape from Kravica, and I came here this morning. That's what he told me. He told me about how my father was captured. They stormed Kravica, and then they tried to flee Kravica and get to the Drina River. My father ran behind the school. There was a bulldozer that was parked behind the school building. He hid behind one of the big tyres. A Muslim noticed him, however, approached him from the back, and struck him over the head with a rifle butt. My father fell unconscious. And then Mijo Gavric said, I managed to get out but he was stuck there. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this person tell you, give you a description of -- I'll rephrase the question. When you say a Muslim noticed him, did this person give you any additional information about this Muslim? Was this a -- how was this person dressed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that this person was in a camouflage uniform, the kind that was worn by UNPROFOR at the time, or SFOR, if you like. He had an automatic rifle. He approached him from the back, hit him on the head with a rifle butt, and he fell unconscious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were called to -- contacted to identify your father's body?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, in October, when Serbs were found who had been in the Srebrenica prison, I was summoned to take over the body of my father. I arrived. There were quite a number of people there. I reported to the person in charge, and he brought me to see the doctor who had carried out the post-mortem, Dr. Stankovic from Belgrade. I introduced myself as Kostadin Popovic's son, and he said, Well, here is Kostadin's body. It was in a body bag. I asked whether I could see my father's body, and he said, There's no need for you to do it. Just remember him the way it was. And I said that, Well, I would still like to look just to reassure myself that this indeed my father. So he opened the body bag, and I realised immediately that four of his front teeth had been knocked out. He had a gold tooth that was still there. And then he explained everything to me and showed me around. He showed that the skull had been shattered and the chest too. He said, You see that a part of it was broken off. Some of the ribs were fractured, as well as the arms. I said, Doctor, can you please just close the bag, and I started to cry. I picked up the body. A car came by and took the body to Kravica. It was after Christmas when I had found him, together with my grandfather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone with respect to your father about where he was following his capture?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of my family and my uncle, we kept visiting the command to ask questions about him. We never received any information whatsoever until our neighbour, Ratko Nikolic, was exchanged, and then we knew exactly that on the 6th of February he had died in prison. At the command for a while they would tell us that he was still alive, and at other times they would tell us that he was dead. We knew nothing for certain until Ratko Nikolic, a neighbour of ours from Kravica, was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to hand out some documents that I will have the witness take a look at, and if we can have a number assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break -- we're due to have a break in two or three minutes' time, so are you ready to have a break now or can you dispose of this in two or three minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I think it's best we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a break, Mr. Siller. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I address very briefly the request you made, and indeed I can be very short on this. We have no objection to the lifting of the label of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are deciding here and now orally that the confidentiality that was attached to the two documents which have been admitted, which are statements effectively admitted in evidence under Rule 92 bis (C), is being lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In that respect, Your Honour, I would like to tender these two statements. May I have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had the others been given a number already or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these will be given a number. You need to tell me what the subsequential number is because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 456. So for the record, the statement by Veseljko Bogicevic, dated the 20th of July, 2000, which has just been tendered and which had previously already been admitted as an exhibit under Rule 92 bis (C), is being resubmitted by the Prosecution without the confidentiality that previously attached to the same document, and it is hereby being marked Prosecution Exhibit P456. 456. The same applies to the other document, which is a statement made by Miladin Bogdanovic, a gentleman born on the 21st of October, 1934, in Jezestica, Bratunac municipality, the statement bearing the date of the 28th of May of the year 2000. This is being now marked as Prosecution Exhibit P457. Yes, with regard to the rest of the information that you had to verify about the Zvornik inquest papers? Any news?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, we do have some partial news. We were able to verify that we did send a request for this file. We are now waiting on confirmation that the files were never given to us by the Bosnian authorities. So what we do have is confirmation that it was a -- a request was made. We don't have, and this is an official RFA by the Office of the Prosecution. But what we are waiting for now is their response to us, or lack thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you think you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate less than an hour. I could possibly finish before. That's a very good possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two hours, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move -- try to cut it as short as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. If I could the usher's assistance, and I don't know if this particular document was already given a number, that was just handed out prior to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will verify with the registrar. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because he had just taken them in his hands when we decided to have the break, so I don't recall even seeing these documents before we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I will, just for the record, state that documents were handed up to the Court. There is a B/C/S and English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because the stapler -- let me verify this, because I had a staple here or a clip which got loose and I may have a confusion. The first ERN page of the original document in Serbo-Croat, is it 0359-3124?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And does it -- and with 0359-3173?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wish to state that we strenuously challenge the authenticity of this document for reasons which will become clear very soon. But I do not wish to discuss this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam Vidovic. The English version has ERN number 0 -- it doesn't have an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, it should be to the top right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the ERN -- the first page and the last page -- that's the first page, and the last page of the Bosnian Serb --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the same ERN number. I did inquire about this before. It evidently was not given an additional ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but even at first sight, this seems to be thicker than this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, possibly because of translation and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it has the same sequence of -- numerical sequence. Anyway, let's move. If there will be a problem, we'll face it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P458.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being received and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P458.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask that the usher present this document, the original document, the B/C/S version of it, to Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, please take a look at this document. Do you recognise what's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we have an explanation as to what this is about, what sort of diary or log book is this, whose is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, stop, stop, stop. That's not regular. Don't interrupt again in this manner. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Oh, I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when is the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was supposed to give a statement about my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gave you this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My uncle, who lives in Milici, Radovan Popovic. And he got it from a next-door neighbour who had a cafe and who knew my late father because they had worked together in Milici. When he read this and saw the name, Popovic Risto Kostadin, he gave this document to my uncle. My uncle had this document, and when we received the summons to testify about my father, I called him up and I said to him, Uncle, and he said he had documents that he got from his next-door neighbour. I asked him where it was, and he said, It's at my home. And that's how I got this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did your uncle give it to you? Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two months ago, when I made the statements about my late father and grandfather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do with the document? Let me just rephrase this question. Are you sure it's two months ago? Because we're now in December. Was it in October or was it before?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was, but I gave it to the people who were questioning me about my father, and these people were from The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did he first learn about the existence of this document? When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was about to be interviewed about my father, that's when I called up my uncle and then he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when your uncle received it from the gentleman that has the cafe?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got this document a long time ago. He kept it at his home, but he didn't do anything about it. He just kept it at home and read what it said, and he read the list of names. He got this a long time ago, and it was there at his home, just sitting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where he got it, where he obtained this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got the document from the owner of this cafe. And the cafe owner, he knew my late father; they had worked together in Milici. And he was my uncle's next-door neighbour. He gave it to him to read, and so this document stayed with my uncle, at his home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, can we have some names, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you -- do you recall the names -- what's your uncle's name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Popovic. He is a building construction engineer, civil engineer, and he works in the Milici municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person from the cafe who gave it to your uncle, do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Radan Erkic. Eric or Erkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for sake of clarification, is this the same -- the owner of the cafe, is this the same person that worked with your father in Milici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the bauxite mine in Milici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when, and from where, he obtained this document, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who had a work obligation in Milici, they were working on the electric power line, they were putting up the cables, and they would come into his cafe. They knew about my father because he'd worked there for a long time. They knew he'd been taken prisoner, and they read his name there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But what we're trying to establish is where the person who first gave it to your uncle, where he received the documents, if you know. If you don't know, just let us know that you do not.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got it from those people who were sitting there in his cafe. They read the document and they left it with him in the cafe. And then the cafe owner gave it to my uncle. And it stayed with my uncle until the time came --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the names of the people who gave it to the person who owned the cafe?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where they got this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were all people from Milici, as I said, and they were working on the electric power line, the cables. And they found this document thrown away in a meadow. And they looked at it, they read it, and then they arrived in the cafe owned by my uncle's next-door neighbour. And they knew my late father because he'd worked in the Milici mine for 10 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this document end up in the cafe this year, or prior? In 2004 or was it prior, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was much earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, do you have an idea who could have kept this diary, who kept this diary? Do you have an idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a stamp here, and it says "Military Police" and there's a signature here. It's all written down here. There are various stamps and signatures here. Avdo Huseinovic. This is this document. There is a stamp here. It says "Srebrenica Military Police."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know this person, Avdo Huseinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he's still alive or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any reference to your father in this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just in the interests of time, Your Honour, I would ask the witness to look at page 47, and in the English translation, page 31. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Popovic, if you take a look at page 47 of this document, can you tell us if you -- if this is referring to your father, Kostadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Popovic, son of Risto, Kostadin, mother's name, Vidosava Milanovici from Opravdici, married to Mila Krsmanovic from Koprivna. Yes. Yes, this is the document -- a document that mentions my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this information about your father; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page there's reference to Ratko Nikolic, and if you would look at that part of the document that indicates --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based on what you know of Mr. Nikolic, is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we can skip that, Ms. Richardson. I think we can assess that on the basis of the testimony of the previous witness, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, the document also indicated that there's information here that your father was arrested near the school in Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than Mr. Nikolic, do you see any other names here on this page or on page 47 that refers to anyone that you know was -- that was imprisoned with your father?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milisava Nikolic. Let me just find it. It's not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may want to take a -- it's page 30 on the English document.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Nikolic Milisava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this person also imprisoned with your father?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether she was imprisoned together with my father, but she was taken prisoner in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
